newsitem.title: PERU: Peru holds line in 94th day of hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru holds line in 94th day of hostage crisis.

text.p: Peru held its tough negotiating line against Marxist hostage-takers as the Lima crisis entered its 94th day on Friday with little evidence that a solution is nearing, despite diplomatic activity.

Dampening speculation of behind-the-scenes dealing, President Alberto Fujimori sternly denied he would free jailed Marxist rebels in exchange for the release of 72 dignitaries held at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

"I absolutely, totally and flatly deny that my government's position has changed," Fujimori said, repeating his rejection of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) demand for the freedom of some 450 detained comrades.
"There will be no freeing of MRTA prisoners," he added during a visit on Thursday to the central Andes.

Speculation had been rife that Fujimori agreed at a meeting this week with Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to free some MRTA prisoners as a way of persuading the 20 rebels to end their action.

"The security of the country comes before any other interest. I'm sorry if that sounds hard," added Fujimori, saying any release of MRTA prisoners would set a dangerous precedent for a country ravaged by violence since 1980 by the MRTA and larger Maoist guerrilla group, the Shining Path.

"Perhaps for other countries, this might not have so much meaning and they may seek solutions that don't take this into account, but we Peruvians have suffered for 15 years and we've had 25,000 deaths," he said.
Tokyo's envoy Komura, on a three-country tour aimed to speed a peaceful solution to the crisis, was due to meet on Friday with the president of the Dominican Republic, Leonel Fernandez.
He flew into the Dominican Republic late on Thursday from Cuba, where President Fidel Castro confirmed his offer of asylum for the MRTA members if a deal is struck in Lima.
Fernandez's government has also tentatively offered to take some of the hostage-takers if necessary.
MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa has ruled out asylum, saying the rebels want to stay in Peru and return to their jungle stronghold after winning the release of their prisoners.
But in a possibly significant shift, an MRTA spokesman, speaking on Thursday via walkie-talkie from the residence, said the group had no comment on the asylum request.

The MRTA met on Thursday in the besieged compound with two members of a mediation panel overseeing negotiations with the government -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent.
But the pair made no comment after the two-hour meeting, and there was no word if more talks were scheduled for Friday.

The three-man mediating panel, which also includes the Vatican's representative, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, is holding separate meetings with both sides as part of a period of "reflection" since the last and tenth round of face-to-face talks March 12.
The government has said it will only use force if the hostages are harmed, but is known to be training crack troops around a mock-up of the residence in case of an assault.

Fujimori's army claims to have captured 38 MRTA members in a sweep of the group's central jungle stronghold. The MRTA and leading human rights group Aprodeh, however, say innocent peasants and not rebels were victimised in the sweep.
Adding to the tension, leaked intelligence documents said the MRTA has slipped another 50 fighters into Lima to lend armed support to the group holding the diplomatic compound.

The military and anti-terrorist police intelligence reports obtained by Reuters, both marked secret, said the MRTA members, led by a woman rebel leader with the nom de guerre "La Gringa," arrived from strongholds in the central jungle.

They would be used to carry out attacks on government and diplomatic posts, or media headquarters, as a way to support the hostage-takers, said the military intelligence report dated Feb. 21 and sent to Armed Forces chief Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza Rios.
